lessons.title: Personal Hygiene for Food Handlers
lessons.body: As a peanut butter producer, your body can be the biggest source of contamination. You must wash your hands thoroughly with soap and warm water for at least 20 seconds before starting work, after using the toilet, after coughing or sneezing, and after handling raw materials or waste. Keep fingernails short and clean; no nail polish or artificial nails because they can harbor bacteria. Cover any cuts or sores with a waterproof bandage and a clean glove. Wear clean clothing and a clean apron daily. If you have a beard, wear a beard net; otherwise, a hairnet is mandatory to prevent hair from falling into the product. Avoid jewelry like rings, earrings, and watches because they can trap dirt and fall into food. Do not eat, drink, smoke, or chew gum in the production area. If you are sick with diarrhea, vomiting, fever, or open wounds, stay home and do not handle food. When you sneeze or cough, do so away from the product and into a tissue or your elbow, then wash your hands again. Use a clean handkerchief or tissue, and never wipe your nose with your hands. Also, keep your hands away from your face, hair, and mouth. These habits protect your product from harmful bacteria like Salmonella and E. coli, which can make your customers seriously ill. Remember, your customers trust you to provide safe food. By following these simple rules, you show respect for their health and build a reputation for quality. In many African communities, word of mouth is powerful; a single case of food poisoning can ruin your business. So make personal hygiene a daily priority, not just a one-time task.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Sanitizing Equipment and Work Area
lessons.body: Cleaning and sanitizing are two different steps: cleaning removes visible dirt, grease, and food particles, while sanitizing kills harmful bacteria. You need both. Start by scraping off leftover peanut paste from equipment like grinders, mixers, and bowls. Then wash with warm water and dish soap, using a brush or cloth to scrub all surfaces, including corners and crevices. Rinse with clean water. Next, sanitize using a food-safe sanitizer. You can make a cheap sanitizer by mixing 1 tablespoon of unscented bleach in 4 liters of clean water. Soak equipment for at least 1 minute, then air dry on a clean rackâdo not dry with a cloth, as it can recontaminate. For work surfaces, clean and sanitize before and after each production session. Use dedicated cleaning cloths and replace them daily. Floors should be swept and mopped with soapy water, then sanitized. Walls and ceilings should be wiped down weekly to prevent dust and mold. Keep pests out by storing ingredients in sealed containers, fixing leaks, and removing trash daily. Set a cleaning schedule: after each batch, clean the grinder and mixer; daily, clean all surfaces and floors; weekly, deep clean walls and vents. Use a checklist to track tasks. Remember, dirty equipment can grow mold and bacteria that produce off-flavors and toxins. A clean workspace also prevents cross-contamination between raw peanuts and finished paste. In hot African climates, bacteria multiply quickly, so clean and sanitize at least twice a day if you produce continuously. Invest in a few dedicated brushes, buckets, and sanitizerâit's cheaper than losing customers to foodborne illness.

lessons.title: Safe Food Handling: Preventing Contamination
lessons.body: Contamination can happen at any point: from raw peanuts to the final jar. To prevent it, separate raw and finished products. Store raw peanuts in clean, covered containers away from the finished paste. Use separate utensils and equipment for raw and finished products; if not possible, clean and sanitize between uses. Never put finished paste back into a container that held raw peanuts. Keep pests out by sealing all openings, using screens on windows and doors, and storing trash in covered bins away from production. Control moisture: peanuts and paste absorb moisture, which promotes mold growth. Store in a dry place, ideally below 60% humidity. Use food-grade containers and avoid using containers that previously held chemicals. When handling paste, use clean, sanitized scoops or spoonsânever your hands. If you must touch the product, wear clean gloves. Avoid cross-contamination from allergens: if you also process other nuts, clean equipment thoroughly between batches. Label all containers with contents and date. Practice FIFO (First In, First Out): use older stock first. During production, keep the area free of unnecessary items. If you drop paste on the floor, discard it. Do not use fallen peanuts. Also, ensure that water used for cleaning is potable. In many African settings, water can be contaminated; if unsure, boil it first or use filtered water. Finally, train all workers on these rules and supervise them. A simple mistake like using a dirty cloth can contaminate a whole batch. By following these steps, you protect your product from bacteria, mold, and allergens, ensuring it is safe to eat.

lessons.title: Aflatoxin Testing and Control Measures
lessons.body: Aflatoxins are poisons produced by molds that can grow on peanuts, especially in hot, humid conditions. They can cause liver cancer and are especially dangerous for children. To control aflatoxins, start at the farm: buy peanuts from farmers who practice good agricultural practices, such as drying peanuts properly and storing them in dry, ventilated areas. Reject any peanuts that are discolored, moldy, or shriveled. At your facility, sort peanuts by hand or machine to remove damaged and moldy kernels. Store peanuts in a dry place with less than 10% moisture content. Use clean, dry sacks on pallets, away from walls. Test your peanuts and finished paste for aflatoxins. You can use a simple test kit like ELISA or lateral flow strips, which are available in many African countries. These kits cost about $5-10 per test and give results in 10-20 minutes. Test each batch of raw peanuts and finished paste. If aflatoxin levels exceed 10 ppb (parts per billion) for total aflatoxins (or 5 ppb for aflatoxin B1), do not use or sell the product. Instead, discard it safely or use it for non-food purposes like animal feed after consulting authorities. Keep records of test results. If you cannot afford test kits, work with local laboratories or cooperatives that offer testing services. Also, control moisture during storage and production. Use dehumidifiers if available, or store in airtight containers with desiccant packs. Never mix contaminated peanuts with good ones. By testing and controlling aflatoxins, you protect your customers and your business. Remember, aflatoxin poisoning is cumulative; even small amounts over time can harm health. So make testing a routine part of your quality control.

lessons.title: Record Keeping for Quality Control
lessons.body: Record keeping is not just paperworkâit's your tool to trace problems, prove quality, and improve. Start with a simple notebook or a spreadsheet on a phone or computer. For each batch of peanut butter, record: date of production, batch number, quantity produced, source of peanuts (farmer or supplier), aflatoxin test result, cleaning and sanitizing done, and any deviations. Also, keep records of supplier information, including contact details and delivery dates. For equipment, log cleaning and maintenance. For personal hygiene, keep a daily checklist signed by each worker. For training, record who was trained and when. These records help you identify trends: if a batch spoils, you can trace back to the supplier or a cleaning issue. They also show customers and inspectors that you are serious about safety. Keep records for at least one year, or as required by local regulations. Store them in a dry, safe place. Use a simple format: a table with columns for date, batch, activity, result, and signature. If you use a phone, take photos of records as backup. In many African countries, food safety inspectors may ask for records during certification. Having them ready can mean the difference between passing and failing. Also, records help you calculate costs and reduce waste. For example, if you notice that batches from a certain supplier often fail aflatoxin tests, you can switch suppliers. So make record keeping a habit, not a chore. It takes only a few minutes per batch but pays off in safety and reputation.

lessons.title: Government Food Safety Standards and Certification
lessons.body: Every country has food safety laws and standards that you must follow to sell peanut butter legally. These are set by government agencies like the national bureau of standards, ministry of health, or food and drug authority. In Kenya, for example, the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) sets standards for peanut butter, including limits for aflatoxins, moisture, and microbial contamination. In Nigeria, the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) regulates food products. You need to register your product and obtain a certificate of analysis from an accredited lab. The process usually involves: submitting an application, providing product samples for testing, passing an inspection of your facility, and paying fees. Requirements vary, but common ones include: a clean production area, proper sanitation, aflatoxin testing, labeling with ingredients, net weight, production and expiry dates, and your contact details. Certification shows customers that your product meets safety and quality standards, which can boost sales. It also opens doors to larger markets, like supermarkets and export. To prepare, contact your local standards office or food safety authority to get the specific requirements. They may offer training or guidelines. You may also need to have a food handler's certificate for each worker, which involves a medical test and training. Keep your certification up to date; renewals are usually annual. Even if certification is not mandatory for small-scale sales, following the standards is good practice. It protects your customers and your business. In the long run, investing in certification can pay off through increased trust and market access. So take the first step: visit your local office and ask what you need to do.

quiz.q: What is the minimum time you should wash your hands with soap and water?
quiz.explanation: Washing for at least 20 seconds helps remove harmful bacteria and viruses.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT allowed in the production area?
quiz.explanation: Chewing gum can contaminate food and is not allowed in food handling areas.

quiz.q: What should you do if you have a cut on your hand?
options: B) Cover with a waterproof bandage and glove
C) Wash it with water only
quiz.explanation: Covering cuts prevents bacteria from entering the food.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid wearing jewelry in food production?
options: B) It can trap dirt and fall into food
D) It can react with peanuts
quiz.explanation: Jewelry can harbor bacteria and become a physical hazard if it falls into food.

quiz.q: When should you stay home from work?
options: A) When you have a headache
B) When you have diarrhea or vomiting
D) When you have a runny nose
quiz.explanation: Diarrhea and vomiting can indicate a contagious illness that can be spread through food.

quiz.q: What is the difference between cleaning and sanitizing?
options: B) Cleaning removes dirt; sanitizing kills bacteria
C) Sanitizing removes dirt; cleaning kills bacteria
D) Cleaning is for floors; sanitizing is for equipment
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes visible dirt, while sanitizing reduces bacteria to safe levels.

quiz.q: How can you make a simple sanitizing solution?
options: A) 1 tablespoon bleach in 1 liter water
B) 1 tablespoon bleach in 4 liters water
C) 1 cup bleach in 4 liters water
D) 1 cup bleach in 1 liter water
quiz.explanation: A ratio of 1 tablespoon unscented bleach to 4 liters of water is a common food-safe sanitizer.

quiz.q: After sanitizing equipment, how should you dry it?
options: C) Air dry on a clean rack
quiz.explanation: Air drying prevents recontamination from cloths.

quiz.q: How often should you clean and sanitize work surfaces?
options: C) Before and after each production session
quiz.explanation: Frequent cleaning and sanitizing prevents bacterial growth and cross-contamination.

quiz.q: What is a key reason to keep pests out of the production area?
options: B) They can contaminate food with bacteria
quiz.explanation: Pests like rodents and insects can carry harmful bacteria and contaminate food.

quiz.q: What is the best way to prevent cross-contamination between raw peanuts and finished paste?
options: C) Use separate utensils and equipment
D) Wash utensils with water only
quiz.explanation: Separate utensils and equipment prevent bacteria from raw peanuts from contaminating the finished product.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using your hands to handle finished paste?
options: C) It is faster to use hands
D) Hands make the paste oily
quiz.explanation: Hands can transfer harmful bacteria to the paste; use clean scoops or gloves.

quiz.q: What does FIFO stand for in food storage?
quiz.explanation: FIFO means using older stock first to prevent spoilage.

quiz.q: What should you do if you drop peanut paste on the floor?
options: A) Pick it up and use it
C) Wash it and use it
quiz.explanation: Floor surfaces can be contaminated; dropped food must be discarded.

quiz.q: What is aflatoxin?
options: B) A poison produced by molds
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxins are toxic compounds produced by certain molds, especially on peanuts.

quiz.q: What is the maximum safe level of total aflatoxins in peanut butter for human consumption?
quiz.explanation: Many countries set a limit of 10 ppb for total aflatoxins in food.

quiz.q: How can you reduce aflatoxin risk at the farm level?
options: B) Dry peanuts properly and store in dry conditions
C) Store peanuts in humid place
D) Mix good and bad peanuts
quiz.explanation: Proper drying and dry storage prevent mold growth and aflatoxin production.

quiz.q: What should you do with peanuts that are moldy or discolored?
options: B) Sort them out and discard
quiz.explanation: Moldy peanuts likely contain aflatoxins and should be removed.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for aflatoxin?
quiz.explanation: ELISA or lateral flow test kits are commonly used for aflatoxin testing.

quiz.q: If a batch of peanut paste tests above the safe limit for aflatoxin, what should you do?
options: D) Label it as low quality
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin-contaminated food must not be sold; it should be discarded or used for non-food purposes.

quiz.q: Why is record keeping important for quality control?
options: A) It helps trace problems and prove quality
B) It is required by law only
C) It takes too much time
quiz.explanation: Records help identify sources of contamination and demonstrate compliance with standards.

quiz.q: What information should be recorded for each batch?
options: A) Date, batch number, quantity, supplier, test results
quiz.explanation: Complete batch records enable traceability and quality control.

quiz.q: How long should you keep food safety records?
quiz.explanation: Most regulations require records to be kept for at least one year.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of keeping records?
options: A) It helps identify trends and reduce waste
C) It is required for certification
quiz.explanation: Records serve multiple purposes, including quality improvement and compliance.

quiz.q: What does a food safety certification show?
options: A) That your product meets safety and quality standards
B) That your product is expensive
C) That you have a large business
D) That you use organic peanuts
quiz.explanation: Certification demonstrates compliance with established food safety standards.

quiz.q: Which agency in Kenya sets food standards?
quiz.explanation: The Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) is responsible for food standards in Kenya.

quiz.q: What is a common requirement for food certification?
quiz.explanation: Certification typically requires meeting multiple criteria including hygiene, testing, and labeling.

quiz.q: Why is certification beneficial for your business?
options: A) It boosts customer trust and market access
C) It is mandatory for all
D) It is only for export
quiz.explanation: Certification can increase consumer confidence and open larger markets.

quiz.q: What should you do before selling peanut butter in your country?
options: A) Check local food safety regulations
quiz.explanation: It is essential to understand and comply with local food safety laws.

quiz.q: What is a food handler's certificate?
options: A) A certificate showing you have been trained in food safety
B) A certificate for owning a food business
C) A certificate for exporting food
D) A certificate for organic farming
quiz.explanation: A food handler's certificate is issued after training and medical screening for food handlers.
